statement: In the United States, law-enforcement seizure records and overdose death records describe counterfeit pills taking a growing part in fentanyl exposure from 2018 to 2021, comparing the first with the last quarter of each period; neither source tested what share of pills sold on the street contain fentanyl. In quarterly records from the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas programme (33 designated trafficking areas, in 50 states and the District of Columbia, whose participating federal, state, local and tribal agencies report their seizures), seizures in which any fentanyl or fentanyl analogue was detected rose between January–March 2018 and October–December 2021 from 424 to 1,539 for powders and from 68 to 635 for pills. Pills were thus 13.8% of these pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures at the start and 29.2% at the end (68 of 492 and 635 of 2,174, editors' calculation); the authors' conclusion that 'over a quarter of fentanyl seizures are now in pill form' refers to this share of seizures, not to the share of pills that held fentanyl. The number of fentanyl-containing pills seized in a quarter rose from 42,202 to 2,089,186, partly because pill seizures grew larger (about 621 pills per pill seizure at the start and about 3,290 at the end, editors' calculation). Read from the figures, all four counts were higher in April–June or July–September 2021 than in the last quarter, while the pill share was at its highest in the last quarter. The records hold nothing on what the pills were made to look like, how much fentanyl they held, what else they contained or where in the country the changes happened, and seizures reflect policing, testing and reporting as well as supply, which the authors acknowledge (Palamar et al., 2022). In death records from 30 jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia) in CDC's State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System, the share of unintentional or undetermined-intent overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use was 2.0% in July–September 2019 and 4.7% in October–December 2021 (106,293 deaths over the period), after a high of about 5.1% in April–June 2021 (read from the figure); in the eight western jurisdictions it went from 4.7% to 14.7%, their highest quarter, and it stayed below 4% in the other regions. Evidence of counterfeit pill use meant any of: pills at the scene identified as counterfeit; pills that tested positive for drugs other than what they appeared to contain; pills that looked like oxycodone or alprazolam when that drug was absent on post-mortem toxicology; unmarked pills; or a witness report of pill use when no drug detected exists as a legitimate pill. It was coded from death-investigation narratives; how many pills were tested in a laboratory is not reported; the authors expect it to be undercounted, unevenly within and between jurisdictions; and some pills found at a scene may not have been used. In 2021, in 35 jurisdictions, 2,437 of 54,768 overdose deaths (4.4%) had such evidence: of counterfeit oxycodone only in 1,346 (55.2%; pills marked 'M-30' documented in 889 of them), of counterfeit alprazolam (Xanax) only in 415 (17.0%, editors' calculation), of both in 95 (3.9%) and of an unspecified type in 581 (23.8%, editors' calculation); 55.8% of them were in western jurisdictions, against 16.3% of other overdose deaths. Illicitly manufactured fentanyls were listed as a cause of 93.0% of the deaths with such evidence against 72.2% of other overdose deaths, and as the only drugs listed (alcohol not counted) in 41.4% against 19.5%; illicit benzodiazepines in 5.3% against 1.4%, and in 17.1% of the deaths with evidence of counterfeit alprazolam only. These are drugs listed as causes of death, not the contents of tested pills; the authors infer that the pills used likely contained the drugs that caused death (O'Donnell et al., 2023). The one drug-checking study read, at two supervised consumption sites in Vancouver in 2017–2018, tested mostly powders and very few pills (no number given) and reports no results by form, so it gives no figures for pills (Tupper et al., 2018). How well fentanyl test strips detect fentanyl is a separate answer (see the answers on fentanyl test strips). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Are fake pills with fentanyl getting more common? In the US up to 2021, two kinds of records say yes, though neither tested what share of street pills hold fentanyl. Of police seizures that held fentanyl, pills were 14 in 100 in early 2018 and 29 in 100 in late 2021; the rest were powder. Fentanyl pills seized in three months went from about 42,000 to about 2.1 million, partly because seizures got bigger. In death records from 29 states and Washington, DC, the share of overdose deaths with signs that fake pills were used went from 2 in 100 in mid-2019 to about 5 in 100 by mid-2021 and then stayed about there; in western states it went from about 5 to about 15 in 100. In 2021, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30', and 17 in 100 fake alprazolam (Xanax) only. Fentanyl or similar drugs were among the recorded causes of 93 in 100 of them. Police seizures depend on what police look for and test, death records probably miss many fake pills, and a drug-checking study in Vancouver tested too few pills to say anything about them.
population: Fentanyl-containing drug seizures recorded by law-enforcement agencies taking part in the 33 US High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (50 states and the District of Columbia), 2018–2021; unintentional and undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths with a medical examiner or coroner report in 30 US jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia), July 2019 to December 2021, and in 35 jurisdictions in 2021; and samples brought for drug checking at two supervised consumption sites in Vancouver, Canada, 2017–2018
exposure: Pill form, against powder form, among fentanyl-containing seizures; documented evidence of counterfeit pill use among overdose deaths
comparator: The first against the last quarter of each period, with no statistical test of the death-record trend; for 2021, overdose deaths without such evidence in the same jurisdictions; census regions
outcome: Quarterly counts of fentanyl-containing powder and pill seizures, the pill share of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures and the number of pills seized; the quarterly share of overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use, the pill imitated and the drugs listed as causes of death

No tests or intervals. Tupper et al. (2018): very few pills tested (no number), no results by form.

evidence.extracted: Jurisdictions in CDC's State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS) entered unintentional and undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths from death certificates, post-mortem toxicology and medical examiner or coroner reports. Trends used the 30 jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia) with complete data for July 2019 to December 2021, and the 2021 characteristics 35 jurisdictions; four states (five in 2021) reported only from counties with at least 75% of their 2017 overdose deaths; analysis was restricted to deaths with a medical examiner or coroner report. Deaths were flagged by a counterfeit-pill checkbox or by text searches of the narrative (for example for 'counterf' or 'M-30', or for oxycodone or alprazolam brand names when that drug was absent on toxicology), and flagged narratives were coded by two coauthors. Evidence of counterfeit pill use was any of: pills at the scene identified as counterfeit by witnesses, police, medical examiners or coroners; pills testing positive for drugs other than what they appeared to contain; oxycodone- or alprazolam-looking pills with that drug absent on post-mortem toxicology; unmarked pills; or a witness report of pill use when none of the drugs detected exists in legitimate pill form. How many deaths met each criterion, or involved laboratory-tested pills, is not reported.

risk_of_bias.note: Coverage and measurement could materially change the figures. The seizure series depends on which agencies reported and what they tested, neither of which is described, and on policing priorities, and it is reported only at its first and last quarters (card sc_palamar_2022: JBI, moderate as a description of recorded seizures, high as an indicator of supply). Evidence of counterfeit pill use in deaths depends on how completely death investigators documented pills, which the authors expect to vary within and between jurisdictions, rarely rests on pills known to have been tested, and may have been documented more fully as awareness of counterfeit pills grew, which would inflate the rise (the editors' concern, not tested; card sc_odonnell_2023: JBI moderate).

inconsistency.note: The two record systems agree in direction; they measure different things, and the statement does not compare their sizes.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: records of seizures and of deaths with documented evidence, not the contents of pills sold on the street, which the statement says neither source tested; US only, to 2021.

imprecision.note: Large record sets (hundreds to thousands of seizures a quarter; 106,293 and 54,768 deaths); no intervals are printed, but chance is not the main concern.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for surveillance series; not suspected.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (counts, shares and their change over time in records): starts low, is never upgraded, and is downgraded one level for risk of bias because coverage and measurement could materially change the figures (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias are not downgraded. Very low. Status replicated: two independent record systems, run by different teams, agree in direction (pills became a larger part of US fentanyl seizures in 2018–2021, and deaths with evidence of counterfeit pills a larger share of overdose deaths in 2019–2021); each figure comes from one source, the two measure different things and their sizes cannot be compared, and O'Donnell et al. cite Palamar et al. without sharing its data. Both are compared first quarter against last quarter, and in both the counts or the total share peaked in mid-2021, which the statement says. The drug-checking study qualifies the claim only by showing that it cannot answer for pills. Nothing here measures the share of street pills that contain fentanyl, how much they hold, or the risk of using a counterfeit pill; the DEA laboratory figures on pill contents that Palamar et al. cite were not read and are not used.

statement: In 62 people recruited by staff of six US overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes in 2005–2006 (in Chicago, New Mexico, San Francisco, Baltimore and two in New York City; 72.6% men, 85.5% currently or formerly using drugs, 22.6% syringe-exchange staff), the 30 trained by the recruiting programme (a median of 8 months before, range 1 to 80 months) compared with the 32 not trained by it were associated with higher scores at recognising opioid overdoses in 16 written scenarios and at deciding when naloxone was called for, scored against the answers of 11 medical experts; trained people still misjudged some opioid overdoses, and both groups often misjudged the scenarios that were not opioid overdoses. The scenarios were experiences that people who inject drugs had described as overdoses in an earlier study; by the experts' combined answers, 9 were opioid overdoses, all calling for naloxone, and 7 were non-opioid overdoses or not overdoses, not calling for it, and respondents could also answer that there was not enough information. Trained respondents recognised on average 7.13 of the 9 opioid overdoses (SD 1.38) against 5.18 (SD 2.55) for untrained respondents (p < 0.001), but 4.63 against 4.28 of the 7 other scenarios (p = 0.42); their totals, 11.77 against 9.47 of 16 (p < 0.005), are 73.6% and 59.2% correct (editors' calculation), not the 85.2% and 68.3% printed in the paper's table and text. Trained respondents chose naloxone in 6.93 of the 9 opioid overdoses against 5.77 (p < 0.05), so on average they did not choose it in about 2 of the 9 against about 3 (2.1 and 3.2 in the paper), and chose it in 0.4 against 1.7 of the 7 scenarios where it was not called for (p < 0.001); naloxone totals were 13.53 against 11.09 of 16 (84.6% and 69.3% correct, p < 0.0001). The experts themselves answered that there was not enough information in 25.6% of their ratings, against 16.0% for trained respondents. The paper reports agreement with the experts as a weighted kappa of 0.85 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.98) for trained and 0.48 (0.18 to 0.77) for untrained respondents, and a kappa of 1.0 for trained respondents' naloxone choices, without saying what was compared; since trained individuals averaged 84.6% correct on naloxone, these figures cannot mean that each trained person matched the experts. All six programmes taught how to tell an opioid overdose from a 'heavy nod', and two explicitly covered non-opioid (for example stimulant) overdoses. The paper gives no results by scenario or by sign and does not print the scenarios, so it cannot show which situations, a heavy nod among them, people got wrong. Programme staff chose who took part and nobody was tested before training, so the difference cannot be credited to training; two of the 11 experts who set the answers are named among the evaluated programmes' staff; the scenarios were written descriptions, not real overdoses; and the paper does not mention fentanyl. The authors' conclusion that 'naloxone training programs are effective and probably cost–effective' rests on this one comparison, with no costs, deaths or real overdoses measured (Green et al., 2008). Whether take-home naloxone programmes lower deaths is a separate answer (see the answer on naloxone programmes). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Would you know if someone was overdosing on opioids? Not always, in the one study read, which used written stories rather than real overdoses. In 2005–2006, staff at six US overdose programmes asked 62 people, most of whom used or had used drugs, to judge 16 short written descriptions of experiences that people who inject drugs had called an overdose; 11 medical experts had decided that 9 were opioid overdoses needing naloxone and 7 were not. People the programmes had trained spotted on average about 7 of the 9 opioid overdoses, and people they had not trained about 5. Trained people still did not choose naloxone in about 2 of the 9 (untrained people about 3), and both groups got only about 4 or 5 of the other 7 right. The experts themselves said there was not enough information in about a quarter of their answers. Staff chose who took part, nobody was tested before training, and the paper does not say which descriptions people got wrong. So it cannot show whether training caused the difference, which signs people miss, or whether people could tell a heavy nod from an overdose, which all six programmes taught.
population: People recruited by staff at six US overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes (Chicago; State of New Mexico; San Francisco; Baltimore; New York City, two programmes), October 2005 to July 2006: 62 respondents, 72.6% men, 85.5% currently or formerly using drugs, 22.6% syringe-exchange staff
exposure: Having been trained in overdose recognition and response by the recruiting programme (a median of 8 months before; trainings of about 15 to 120 minutes)
comparator: People at the same programmes not trained by them (32); and an answer key from 11 medical experts combined by latent class analysis
outcome: Number of 16 written overdose scenarios correctly classified (opioid overdose, or non-opioid overdose or not an overdose) and correctly judged as calling or not calling for naloxone; agreement with the experts (kappa)
magnitude: Green et al. (2008), trained (n = 30) against untrained (n = 32), mean (SD): opioid overdoses recognised 7.13 (1.38) against 5.18 (2.55) of 9, t60 = −3.76, P < 0.001; other scenarios 4.63 (1.40) against 4.28 (1.94) of 7, P = 0.42; recognition total 11.77 (1.92) against 9.47 (3.48) of 16, P < 0.005 (73.6% against 59.2%, editors' calculation; printed as 85.2% against 68.3%); naloxone chosen in opioid overdoses 6.93 (1.76) against 5.77 (2.30) of 9, P < 0.05 (not chosen in 2.1 against 3.2); naloxone correctly not chosen 6.60 (0.72) against 5.32 (1.94) of 7, P < 0.001 (chosen where not called for in 0.4 against 1.7); naloxone total 13.53 (1.96) against 11.09 (2.32) of 16 (84.6% against 69.3%), P < 0.0001. 'Not enough information' in 25.6% of the experts' ratings against 16.0% of trained respondents'. Weighted kappa with the experts 0.85 (0.72–0.98) trained, 0.48 (0.18–0.77) untrained; naloxone kappa 1.0 trained, 0.75 (0.44–1.0) untrained (unit of comparison not stated).

evidence.extracted: The 16 scenarios were experiences that people who inject drugs had described as overdoses, chosen from 60 reported in a study of public injecting; development and validation are reported elsewhere (a 2006 conference abstract). Eleven medical experts classified each as opioid overdose, non-opioid overdose, not an overdose, or not enough information/unsure, and said whether naloxone was indicated; with the non-opioid and non-overdose categories collapsed, latent class analysis of their answers gave the key: 9 opioid overdoses, all requiring naloxone, and 7 non-opioid or non-overdose scenarios, not requiring it. Recognition and naloxone scores each ranged from 0 to 16. No data were gathered on age, race, ethnicity or drugs used. The scenario texts are not printed.

evidence.extracted: Trainings were brief (about 15 to 120 minutes), in settings from syringe exchanges to street corners and private homes, mixing teaching with practice; all covered recognising and responding to opioid overdose and calling 911. evidence.quote: naloxone training programs are effective and probably cost–effective

risk_of_bias.note: A single cross-sectional comparison of groups chosen by programme staff, with no scores before training and no measure of motivation, earlier knowledge, age or drug use; the outcome is answers to unpublished written scenarios, scored against a key partly set by experts who are also programme staff, and staff who knew who was trained could help people fill in the questionnaire (card sc_green_2008: ROBINS-I serious).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: written scenarios, 2005–2006, people recruited at harm-reduction programmes. As an answer about recognising a real overdose today, fentanyl included, it would be rated lower still, which the statement says; the rating is already at its floor.

imprecision.note: 30 and 32 people, but the differences in opioid recognition and in the naloxone totals are large against their spread (P < 0.001 and P < 0.0001); the difference in naloxone choices for the 9 opioid overdoses alone is less precise (P < 0.05).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; no protocol or registration.

grade.reasoning: Observational (a non-randomized comparison of trained and untrained people at one time): starts low; risk of bias −1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Very low. Status single study: no other study of how well people recognise overdose scenarios was read. The claim is worded as an association between having been trained and scores on written scenarios; whether training causes better recognition, how people do at real overdoses, which signs they miss and whether training changes deaths or costs are not shown by this design. The paper's printed recognition percentages do not match its means, and its kappa of 1.0 cannot describe individuals; the statement gives the means and says so. Research findings only: the claim names no signs to look for and no steps to take, which belong to the senior author's emergency guidance (METHODS §8).
